description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

schema.description:

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

tools.name: SearchPlugins
tools.description:
Search the user's claude.ai plugin catalog by keyword. Call this when a plugin (slash command, skill bundle, hook, or agent) from the user's org catalog might help complete the task.

Examples:
- "use the deploy plugin" → keywords ["deploy"]
- "is there something for linting?" → keywords ["lint", "format", "code quality"]

Returns a ranked list with id, name, description, and whether the plugin is already enabled for this session (in a channel session, whether the channel has it). When results fit and SuggestPluginInstall is among your tools, call it to render the install card; otherwise relay the relevant results in text instead. If nothing relevant, proceed without mentioning that you searched.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to [REDACTED_EMAIL]' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

This server helps users set up and manage their Shopify stores.

## Starting a New Business
Users who are still shaping a business can work on it here before they have a store. None of these tools needs one.
- Naming: generate-business-names suggests business names from a short description of what the user sells, who it is for, or the feeling they want.

When the user settles on a name, offer to check domains for it.
Never present a domain as available unless generate-domain-names checked it; a domain you suggest yourself may already be taken.
Follow the user's lead rather than walking them through every step.

## Store Creation
Users who don't have a store yet can use get-new-store-previews to create one from a short description.
After calling get-new-store-previews, encourage the user to browse the previews and pick the theme they like best.
Each preview has a signup link — signing up through it creates a real Shopify store with that theme and matching products pre-installed.
Encourage continued brainstorming: users can try different descriptions, tweak ideas, or explore new directions without commitment.

- Customers: list and search customers.

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. # MillMate

**Less guesswork. More peace of mind.**

MillMate is an AI stock advisor for small rice mills. The mill owner adds their rice brands and types, and notes what comes in and what goes out. MillMate watches the numbers, works out which brand will run out first and which one is piling up, and tells the owner what to do about it in plain English. The owner can also just ask a question, like "What should I order this week?".

Built fresh during ForgeHacks Online 2026 (Business track) and neatHack 2026 (Productivity & Automation track). All code in this repo was written on Oct 10-11, 2026, and the commit history shows it.

## The problem

A mill owner juggles many brands and rice types. Stock lives in notebooks and memory. Running out of a fast seller loses customers. Piling up a slow one ties up cash. Most stock tools are spreadsheets or complex software made for bigger businesses.

## What it does

- Add brands and rice types, and record rice that came in or went out. Big buttons, English only, works on a phone.
- Shows a short story of the day: what needs attention first.
- Gives up to three clear actions, each with the numbers behind it ("proof").
- Answers plain-English questions about the stock.
- Writes a ready-to-copy order note. It never sends anything by itself.
- Shows what the advisor looked at and in what order, so the owner can see how it reached its advice.

## How the agent works

MillMate runs a small observe, reason, decide loop (max 6 steps):

1. **Observe**: reads brands and stock movements (`get_state`).
2. **Reason**: compares brands by days of stock left, recent pace, and piling up (`compare_brands`).
3. **Decide**: picks what to surface and drafts an order note (`draft_reorder`, 3 weeks at the current pace, rounded up to 10 kg).
4. **Check**: every number in the final text is verified against the computed facts. A sentence with a number that does not match is replaced by a safe template sentence.

With an LLM key set, the model chooses the tools through OpenAI-style tool calling. **Without a key the app still works** using a rule-based planner, so it never shows a blank screen. The advice says whether AI was used (`used_ai`).

Every run of the loop is traced with **Neatlogs** (workflow, steps and tool calls), so you can inspect exactly what the agent did.

## Run it

```
pip install -r requirements.txt
uvicorn app.main:app --port 8000
```

Open http://localhost:8000 and press "Try with sample mill" to load demo data.

Optional environment variables (the app works without any of them):

| Variable | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `LLM_API_KEY` | Key for an OpenAI-compatible API (we use Gemini) |
| `LLM_BASE_URL` | e.g. `https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/openai/` |
| `LLM_MODEL` | model name |
| `NEATLOGS_API_KEY` | turns on Neatlogs tracing |

Tests: `pip install pytest && pytest`

## Stack

Python, FastAPI, SQLite, plain HTML/CSS/JS front end, Gemini (optional), Neatlogs, deployed on Render.

## What works and what does not

Works: add and remove brands, record movements, stock math, advice, questions, sample data, tracing, no-key mode.
Not built: user accounts, import from spreadsheets, editing a brand after adding it, sending orders to suppliers. On the free host the database resets when the server restarts, so use the sample mill for demos.

## Honest note on how it was built

Planned and written by the team during the event window with AI coding assistance. No code from earlier projects was reused.

# Crashtest

**Find the bugs your users would hit, before they hit them.**

Most bugs that reach users are not in code nobody tested. They are in paths nobody walked: rejecting instead of approving, the empty account, the second tab, someone else's id in the URL. Crashtest is a macOS app with an autonomous agent that walks those paths for you.

Give it a GitHub repo and it:

1. **Maps the app from its code** — screens, actions, API operations, background jobs, integrations, roles, entity lifecycles, limits.
2. **Writes every scenario a user can do or live through**, ranked P1–P3 and grouped by user journey.
3. **Runs them for real** — clones the app, boots it on your Mac or on your own server (VDS), drives it in a browser, and reports what broke with a screenshot, the root cause at `file:line`, and a suggested diff. It never edits your code.

Built during [neatHack](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon) (Oct 10–12, 2026). Build log: [hackathon.md](hackathon.md).

> 🔴 **Live now:** [watch Crashtest test neatroots](http://34.238.91.131:8080) — every dot is one scenario; the yellow spark is the one being tried right now.

## neatlogs asked us to test their own product

After our first post, neatlogs' head of product engineering [replied](https://x.com/kurokotetsuyami/status/2108943094809071674): *"run this on neatroots, & share your findings with me"*. So we did. Crashtest mapped [neatlogs/neatroots](https://github.com/neatlogs/neatroots) into **581 scenarios across 12 user journeys** in under 5 minutes, booted it on a server by itself, and started running all of them.

The 78 core P1 scenarios: **✅ 56 · ❌ 16 · ⏭ 6**, and every broken verdict checked by hand against the source. Real bugs include a JSON trace with a malformed `resourceSpans` accepted with `200` and silently dropped (`otlp/codec.ts:202`), `retention.days: 0` in `config.yaml` deleting every unpinned run on start (the API rejects 0, the config file does not), and unknown `/api/*` routes answering `200` with the web app's HTML. Each one has repro steps, `file:line` and a one-line fix: [docs/evidence/findings-neatroots.md](docs/evidence/findings-neatroots.md).

![Crashtest × neatroots](docs/evidence/neatroots-findings.png)

## What it found on its first real target

On [TonyMckes/conduit-realworld-example-app](https://github.com/TonyMckes/conduit-realworld-example-app), a well-known RealWorld implementation, Crashtest mapped 39 surfaces into **294 scenarios** across 9 journeys in 143 s, booted the app from scratch (local Postgres, generated `.env`, API + frontend) and ran **every one of them**:

**✅ 180 passed · ❌ 104 broken · ⏭ 10 skipped** — and the 104 broken scenarios trace back to **34 files**. Among them:

- **Saving your settings with a blank password replaces your password.** `backend/controllers/user.js:36` checks `password !== undefined || password !== ""`, which is always true.
- **Any bad, forged or expired token crashes the request with a 500** instead of a 401 — 14 scenarios, one error path in `backend/middleware/authentication.js`.
- **Tokens never expire and survive logout and password changes** (`backend/helper/jwt.js`).
- **A comment can be deleted through any article's URL** — `backend/controllers/comments.js` ignores the slug. Found on the first run and found again, independently, in the full run.
- **Duplicate usernames, self-follows, double-click double-publishes**, negative `limit`/`offset` → 500 with raw DB errors.

We checked the top findings against the source by hand. Details, diffs and screenshots: [docs/evidence/findings-conduit.md](docs/evidence/findings-conduit.md).

It is not tied to one app: on [thedevs-network/kutt](https://github.com/thedevs-network/kutt) (URL shortener) the same build mapped 50 surfaces into **359 scenarios across 11 journeys** in 144 s, then ran all 141 P1 scenarios: **✅ 97 · ❌ 31 · ⏭ 13**. Worst one: deleting a domain "without its links" deletes every link on it, because the checkbox sanitizer passes the string `"false"` through as truthy. [docs/evidence/findings-kutt.md](docs/evidence/findings-kutt.md).

## How it works

```
GitHub link ─► Intake ─► Inventory agent ─► Scenario writer ─► [Start] ─► Local │ VDS
               clone,     Sonnet 5.5,        Haiku 5.5,                     │
               products   read-only tools    parallel per journey           ▼
                                                              Bootstrap agent ─► Sweep agent
                                                              boots the app      one scenario at a time,
                                                              (shell, logs,      Playwright browser + API,
                                                              ports, recovery)   verdict + root cause + diff
```

- **Agents** run on the [Claude Agent SDK](https://docs.claude.com/en/api/agent-sdk/overview) with a per-phase tool set: the inventory agent can only read; the bootstrap and sweep agents operate the app through Crashtest's own MCP tools (`shell`, `start_background`, `read_log`, `expose_port`, `http_get`).
- **Local and VDS are the same to the agent.** Both runtimes implement those tools; the VDS runtime works over SSH and tunnels the app's ports back so the browser on your Mac can drive it.
- **Recovery.** If the app stops answering mid-run, Crashtest restarts it with the commands the bootstrap agent used and carries on. Services run in the foreground and are always stopped at the end, even if you quit mid-run.
- **Chat.** Ask about the app, hand over `.env` values or server details (stored encrypted in the macOS Keychain), or start a run from the conversation.

## Built with the neatHack tools

| Tool | How Crashtest uses it |
|---|---|
| [neatlogs](https://neatlogs.com) | Every phase is its own traced workflow (`repo-inventory`, `scenario-generation`, `app-bootstrap`, `scenario-sweep`, `app-recovery`, `project-chat`), grouped per project. Four custom detections in a "Crashtest agent" group — **Bug found by Crashtest** (108), **Auth or account bug found** (57), **Server error in app under test** (39) and **Unverified verdict** (21) — and before/after traces drove real fixes. Our own build sessions are traced too. [Evidence](docs/evidence/neatlogs-baselines.md) |
| [Entire](https://entire.io) | Checkpoints on our commits ([repo on Entire](https://entire.io/gh/emreozyoruk/crashtest), first checkpoint [`97c75579b386`](https://entire.io/gh/emreozyoruk/crashtest/commit/74641efd901999e96d69fd85f69dde70f3aa0a62)), plus **Entire Graph inside the product**: the inventory and sweep agents get graph search / definitions / callers / blast-radius tools over the repo under test. [Evidence](docs/entire/README.md) |
| [cfo.ai](https://cfo.ai) | [Business plan for Crashtest](https://app.cfo.ai/s/--rWFPOxuMvaL0nN) (read-only link; [Upside](https://app.cfo.ai/s/C9DgOonrAXn3DhqQ), [Downside](https://app.cfo.ai/s/e_GPD5Z-hJGywRX7)): Pro $29 / Cloud $299 pricing, unit costs taken from our neatlogs traces ($0.117 per scenario run, $0.815 per repo inventory), customers → revenue → P&L → cash, and three scenarios. Finding: the first engineer hire decides the runway. [Evidence](docs/cfoai/README.md) |

## Run it

Requirements: macOS, Node 22+, git. Optional: the [Entire CLI](https://entire.io) for graph tools.

```bash
npm install
npm run dev
```

Open **Settings**, add your Anthropic API key (and a GitHub token for private repos, or SSH details for a VDS), then paste a GitHub link into the chat.

# Cube — Payment Failure Resolution Agent

Cube turns a failed payment into a resolved one. When a payment provider reports
a failed charge, Cube opens an **investigation**, classifies the probable cause,
pulls the customer's financial position, recommends a mitigation, runs a
guardrail, and either retries silently, escalates, or emails the customer — with
a human approval step when auto-send is off. Every step is traced and audited.

## How it works

```
provider webhook ─▶ ingest (idempotent) ─▶ queue ─▶ investigation pipeline
                                                         │
   context + history ─▶ cfo.ai financials ─▶ classify ─▶ recommend ─▶ LLM rationale
                                                         │
                              cfo.ai scenario ◀─ audit ─┤
                                                         ▼
                              guardrail ─▶ email sent | queued for approval | blocked | escalate
```

1	=================== Anurag-S1ngh__cube README
2	# Cube — Payment Failure Resolution Agent
3	
4	Cube turns a failed payment into a resolved one. When a payment provider reports
5	a failed charge, Cube opens an **investigation**, classifies the probable cause,
6	pulls the customer's financial position, recommends a mitigation, runs a
7	guardrail, and either retries silently, escalates, or emails the customer — with
8	a human approval step when auto-send is off. Every step is traced and audited.
9	
10	## How it works
11	
12	```
13	provider webhook ─▶ ingest (idempotent) ─▶ queue ─▶ investigation pipeline
14	                                                         │
15	   context + history ─▶ cfo.ai financials ─▶ classify ─▶ recommend ─▶ LLM rationale
16	                                                         │
17	                              cfo.ai scenario ◀─ audit ─┤
18	                                                         ▼
19	                              guardrail ─▶ email sent | queued for approval | blocked | escalate
20	```
21	
22	- **Ingest** (`packages/agent`) is idempotent on the provider event id.
23	- **Classify** maps decline codes + history to a cause, severity and confidence.
24	- **cfo.ai** supplies deterministic financial context and recovery scenarios,
25	  falling back to the local ledger/model when not configured.
26	- **Guardrail** (`packages/agent/src/policy.ts`) always runs before any email:
27	  email present, not risk-flagged, sane amount, per-customer rate limit, quiet
28	  hours.
29	- **Human in the loop**: with `AGENT_AUTO_SEND=false` a passing email is queued
30	  and sent only after an operator approves it.
31	- **Observability**: neatlogs traces span the whole run and are linked from each
32	  investigation.
33	
34	## Stack
35	
36	TypeScript · Bun · Next.js 16 (App Router) · Express 5 · Drizzle ORM ·
37	PostgreSQL · Biome · Turborepo.
38	
39	## Layout
40	
41	```
42	cube/
43	├── apps/
44	│   ├── web/        # Next.js dashboard (investigations, API keys, auth)
45	│   └── server/     # Express API, agent queue, auth, webhooks
46	└── packages/
47	    ├── agent/      # pipeline, classify, policy, cfo.ai + email tools, queue
48	    ├── db/         # Drizzle schema + client
49	    ├── ui/         # shared shadcn/ui primitives
50	    └── config/     # shared tsconfig
51	```
52	
53	## Getting started
54	
55	Prerequisites: [Bun](https://bun.sh), a PostgreSQL database.
56	
57	```bash
58	bun install                 # installs deps and generates env types (varlock)
59	```
60	
61	Configure env (see `.env.schema` in each app for the full list; secrets stay in
62	the gitignored `.env`):
63	
64	- `apps/server/.env` — `DATABASE_URL`, `CORS_ORIGIN`, `SERVER_PUBLIC_URL`,
65	  integrations (`CFO_AI_*`, `NEATLOGS_API_KEY`, `RESEND_API_KEY`, `LLM_*`),
66	  auth (`SESSION_*`, `AUTH_LOGIN_*`).
67	- `apps/web/.env` — `NEXT_PUBLIC_SERVER_URL` and deep-link templates.
68	
69	Apply the schema and seed a demo workspace:
70	
71	```bash
72	bun run db:push             # push the Drizzle schema
73	bun run seed                # demo user + project + API key + webhook secret
74	```
75	
76	`seed` prints the demo login (default `[REDACTED_EMAIL]` / `demo-password`,
77	override with `DEMO_PASSWORD`), an API key and a webhook secret.
78	
79	Run everything in development:
80	
81	```bash
82	bun run dev                 # web on :3001, API on :3000
83	```
84	
85	## Authentication
86	
87	- **Dashboard** uses email + password (Argon2id via `Bun.password`) with an
88	  opaque session token in an httpOnly, SameSite=Lax cookie. Only the token hash
89	  is stored. Register at `/register`, or use the seeded demo user.
90	- **Password reset** emails a single-use, expiring link (`/forgot-password` →
91	  `/reset-password`). Setting a new password revokes every active session.
92	- **Machines** use project API keys (`cube_<prefix>_<secret>`, stored hashed,
93	  revocable, optionally expiring). Send as `Authorization: Bearer …` or
94	  `x-api-key`.
95	- **Tenancy**: every investigation and simulate request is scoped to the
96	  caller's projects — a session sees the projects it owns; an API key sees only
97	  its own project. Manage keys at `/settings/api-keys`.
98	- **Webhooks** are HMAC-SHA256 signed with a per-project secret. Point your
99	  provider at `/webhooks/stripe/:projectId`, or use the global dev secret at
100	  `/webhooks/stripe`.
101	
102	## API (all under the server origin)
103	
104	| Method | Path | Auth | Purpose |
105	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
106	| GET | `/health` | none | Liveness + DB check |
107	| POST | `/auth/register` | none | Create user + workspace, auto-login |
108	| POST | `/auth/login` | none | Email/password login |
109	| POST | `/auth/logout` | session | End the session |
110	| GET | `/auth/me` | session | Current user + projects |
111	| POST | `/auth/password/request` | none | Email a password-reset link |
112	| GET | `/auth/password/verify` | none | Check a reset token (`?token=`) |
113	| POST | `/auth/password/reset` | none | Set a new password from a token |
114	| GET | `/projects` | session | List owned projects |
115	| GET | `/projects/:id/webhook-secret` | session | View webhook URL + secret |
116	| POST | `/projects/:id/webhook-secret` | session | Rotate the webhook secret |
117	| GET/POST/DELETE | `/api-keys[/:id]` | session | List / create / revoke keys |
118	| GET | `/investigations` | session or key | Paginated, filterable list (`page`, `pageSize`, `q`, `status`, `severity`, `sort`, `order`) |
119	| GET | `/investigations/summary` | session or key | KPI aggregates |
120	| GET | `/investigations/:id` | session or key | Full investigation detail |
121	| POST | `/investigations/:id/approve` | session or key | Send a queued email |
122	| POST | `/investigations/:id/reject` | session or key | Reject a queued email |
123	| POST | `/events/failed-payment` | API key | Raise an investigation from your own backend (idempotent) |
124	| GET/POST/DELETE | `/webhook-endpoints[/:id]` | session | Manage outbound webhook endpoints |
125	| GET | `/webhook-endpoints/:id/deliveries` | session | Delivery log for an endpoint |
126	| POST | `/webhooks/stripe[/:projectId]` | HMAC | Provider failed-payment webhook |
127	| POST | `/mock/simulate` | session or key | Fabricate failed charges (dev) |
128	
129	## Integrate from your backend (SDK)
130	
131	Install the typed client (`@cube/sdk`, in `packages/sdk`) and push failed
132	payments from your own billing system — no provider webhook required:
133	
134	```ts
135	import { Cube } from "@cube/sdk";
136	
137	const cube = new Cube({ apiKey: process.env.CUBE_API_KEY! });
138	
139	await cube.events.failedPayment(
140	  {

157	## Outbound webhooks
158	
159	Register endpoints in the dashboard (`/settings/api-keys`) or via
160	`/webhook-endpoints`. Cube POSTs JSON when an investigation moves:
161	`investigation.created`, `investigation.classified`, `investigation.actioned`,
162	`investigation.escalated`, `investigation.resolved`, `email.queued`,
163	`email.sent`, `email.blocked`, `email.failed`.
164	
165	Every request carries a `Cube-Signature: t=<unix>,v1=<hmac-sha256>` header over
166	`"${t}.${rawBody}"`, signed with the endpoint's secret. Deliveries retry with
167	exponential backoff and are logged per endpoint. Verify with the SDK:
168	
169	```ts
170	import { verifyWebhookSignature } from "@cube/sdk";
171	
172	const ok = verifyWebhookSignature(rawBody, req.headers["cube-signature"], secret);
173	```

218	# DealScout
219	
220	Tell it the house you want. It tells you what that house should cost in that area, and which
221	listings beat that price, with proof from each listing's own page.
222	
223	Built solo for [neatHack](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon), 10 to 12 October 2026.
224	
225	## Status
226	
227	DealScout can fetch a listing page politely, save it, and read what the page's own
228	structured data states (rumah123 and 99.co so far). The agents that check that reading
229	are next. This section is updated as the build goes on;
230	`hackathon.md` has the dated log.
231	
232	## Why
233	
234	A tracker of about 4,990 Indonesian house listings, collected automatically over four
235	months, is the starting point. In 100 rows sampled from the later part of it, only 10 had
236	both a land size and a building size, so the rest could not be priced at all. Other sampled
237	rows held bathroom counts of 89 and 205, and a 178 m² house recorded at Rp 165 Juta.
238	
239	In a deal screen, the listing that looks cheapest is often the one that was misread.
240	DealScout checks its own reading of every listing against the source page, and spends the
241	most effort on the listings that look best.
242	
243	## How it works
244	
245	Three agents share one Run:
246	
247	- the **Scout** collects listings and records what each one says,
248	- the **Verifier** re-reads each saved page on a different model, without seeing the
249	  Scout's reasoning,
250	- the **Arbiter** settles any disagreement, or sets the listing aside with the reason.
251	
252	Only confirmed listings are priced against comparable houses or ranked.
253	
254	## Read more
255	
256	- [PLAN.md](PLAN.md): the workflow, the timeline and the evidence the judges check.
257	- [CONTEXT.md](CONTEXT.md): the glossary.
258	- [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md): how several coding agents work in this repo at once.
259	- [hackathon.md](hackathon.md): the build log.
260	
261	## Data and fetching
262	
263	Listing pages are fetched with plain requests that honour each portal's robots.txt and
264	crawl delay. Saved pages stay off this repo because they carry people's names and phone
265	numbers.

279	# Upshift
280	
281	**An autonomous migration agent that finishes what the official codemod can't.**
282	
283	Point it at a Python repo stuck on Pydantic v1. It runs `bump-pydantic`, then
284	lets the interpreter tell it what is still broken, fixes the file that explains
285	the most failures, proves every edit against the whole package and a regression
286	suite, and rolls back anything that doesn't move the number.
287	
288	Built for [neatHack 2026](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon) with **neatlogs**,
289	**Entire** and **cfo.ai**.
290	
291	---
292	
293	## The result
294	
295	Target: [`steamship-core/python-client`](https://github.com/steamship-core/python-client) —
296	199 modules, pinned to `pydantic~=1.10.2`.
297	
298	| | Modules importable | Green tests |
299	|---|---|---|
300	| Pydantic v1 — the ceiling | 198 / 199 | 62 / 62 |
301	| v2, untouched | 31 / 199 | 0 / 62 |
302	| v2 + `bump-pydantic` (official codemod) | **31 / 199** | 0 / 62 |
303	| v2 + `bump-pydantic` + **Upshift** | **RESULT_MODULES** | **RESULT_TESTS** |
304	
305	The codemod exits cleanly, changes 11 files, and **gains zero modules**. It does
306	mechanical renames; it cannot decide that `fetch_if_exists = False` on a model
307	must become `fetch_if_exists: ClassVar[bool] = False` — that takes reading how
308	the attribute is used. That gap is the product.
309	
310	How the metric works, and the baseline measurements:
311	[`bench/baseline-python-client.md`](bench/baseline-python-client.md).
312	
313	## How it works
314	
315	```
316	 bump-pydantic ──▶ import every module ──▶ blame each failure on a file
317	                          ▲                          │
318	                          │                          ▼
319	                   keep or roll back ◀── patch ◀── context
320	                   (imports must rise,          ├─ Entire Graph: definitions & callers
321	                    tests must not fall)        ├─ Entire search: related repo history
322	                                                └─ lessons learned earlier this run
323	```
324	
325	1. **The interpreter drives the work.** Every module is imported in a fresh
326	   process; each failure is blamed on the deepest in-repo frame of its
327	   traceback, and the file that explains the most failures goes first. A regex
328	   over the source can't tell which file is breaking the build — a traceback can.
329	2. **The agent sees the error.** The failing traceback is in the first prompt.
330	   Without it, the model looked at a plausible file and returned it unchanged.
331	3. **Every edit is proven.** A patch is kept only if importable modules rise or
332	   failures blamed on that file fall — and never if importable modules or
333	   passing tests drop. Otherwise it is rolled back and the agent retries with the
334	   new error, up to three times.
335	4. **It can say "not here".** If the cause lives in another file — a base class,
336	   a shared model — the agent answers `NO_CHANGE_NEEDED: <path>` and the loop
337	   follows it.
338	5. **It remembers.** Each accepted file yields one repo-specific lesson, carried
339	   into later prompts and written into the commit as an `Upshift-Lesson:`
340	   trailer, where Entire search can find it on the next run.
341	
342	## The three sponsor tools — and what each one actually does here
343	
344	| | Role | Evidence |
345	|---|---|---|
346	| **neatlogs** | Every LLM call, import check, test run, Graph query and search is a span. Token counts and cost per file come from these traces. | traces tagged by config: NEATLOGS_LINKS |
347	| **Entire Graph** | Before each edit: the definitions, base classes and callers of the models in the file, plus the narrowest covering test. | 583 files, 2,118 symbols, 14,138 relations indexed |
348	| **Entire search** | Recall: related commits from the repo's history and from earlier Upshift runs. | finds e.g. a 2023 commit *"Fix pydantic validators"* |
349	| **Entire Trails** | The migration branch is a Trail; six runners (review, risk, security, drift, confidence, summary) evaluate each push. | TRAIL_LINK |
350	| **cfo.ai** | Ari is connected to the agent's telemetry over MCP and builds pricing and revenue from measured cost — and caught a 2× error in our own cost reporting. | [`BUSINESS.md`](BUSINESS.md) |
351	
352	The chain matters more than any single tool: **Entire** tells the agent where
353	to look, **neatlogs** measures what each decision cost, and **cfo.ai** reads
354	those costs live and turns them into a business.
355	
356	## Ablation: does each tool earn its place?
357	
358	Same target, same model, same starting point. Only the context changes.
359

376	## What broke along the way
377	
378	The agent didn't work until it was measured honestly. Each of these would have
379	put a false number in front of you, and each was found by running it:
380	
381	| Bug | Effect | Fix |
382	|---|---|---|
383	| A pytest collection crash parses as 0 failed / 0 errors | every file recorded as migrated against an empty diff | gate on the import probe, not on pytest alone |
384	| The import probe used `pkgutil.walk_packages` | one broken subpackage reported the whole package as 0/198 | import each module from disk independently |
385	| `entire graph search` called with a positional query | errored, returned `""` — Graph context never reached the agent | `--query`, `--format agent` |
386	| `.entire/` committed on the work branch | `reset --hard` deleted it; Entire went "not set up" mid-run | pin includes `.entire/`; restored on reset |
387	| Files worked alphabetically | correct edits rolled back for not being the current blocker | follow the traceback |
388	| The prompt never contained the error | the blocking file came back "no change" four times | traceback in the first attempt |
389	| Mean cost per file over 4 files, one 10k-token outlier | cost overstated ~2× — **caught by cfo.ai's Ari** | report the median |

431	## Honest notes
432	
433	- **Brain isn't used.** Entire documents a Brain memory feature, but it is not in
434	  CLI 0.11.4. Memory here is built from Entire search plus commit trailers.

454	# Autopsy — a debugger for AI-agent mistakes
455	
456	**Team Last Commit · [neatHack 2026](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon)**
457	
458	Autopsy investigates *why* an AI-agent run failed — not just *where*. It is
459	itself an agent: given a failing run, it combines three evidence sources
460	
461	- **neatlogs traces** — what the failing agent actually did at runtime
462	  (every LLM call, tool call, input, output, error)
463	- **Entire checkpoints** — which coding-agent session produced each commit,
464	  with the transcript of what it was asked to do
465	- **Entire graph** — semantic code search and entity-level per-commit changes
466	
467	and emits an evidence-backed diagnosis: root cause, the exact trace step
468	where it surfaced, the culprit commit **and the session transcript behind
469	it**, plus a suggested fix.
470	
471	The debugger's own investigation is fully traced in neatlogs too — the tool
472	for debugging agents is itself an observable agent.
473	
474	## Why this matters
475	
476	When an agent misbehaves, today's tools show you the *what* (a bad answer, a
477	failed tool call) but not the *why*. The why usually lives in two places at
478	once: the runtime evidence (the trace) and the development history (who
479	changed what, and what they were trying to do). Autopsy is the first tool
480	that joins those two timelines: trace span → suspect code → the checkpoint
481	and coding-agent transcript that introduced it.
482	
483	## Demo result (live, reproducible)
484	
485	We broke a small research agent (`demo_agent`) on purpose: a debugging
486	session flipped `search_docs` from descending to ascending order, so the
487	search tool started returning the *least* relevant pages first. The agent's
488	answer degraded — it could no longer describe the flag of Azerbaijan.
489	
490	Autopsy's diagnosis on the failing trace, verbatim:
491	
492	> **Root cause:** `search_docs` sorts ascending (`reverse=False` at
493	> `demo_agent/app.py:51`), so worst matches come first and the
494	> `flag-of-azerbaijan` page is cut before it reaches the LLM.
495	> **Failing step:** all four `search_docs` calls returned the same three
496	> lowest-scoring pages regardless of query phrasing.
497	> **Culprit:** checkpoint `01M4K1P5A9NYJJNRY2D9XKJ08P` — commit
498	> `dece484` "Flip search_docs ordering for ranking inspection".
499	> **Fix:** `reverse=True`.
500	
501	After the fix commit, the same question produces the full correct answer
502	(*"horizontal tricolour of blue, red, and green, with a white crescent and
503	an eight-pointed star"*).
504	
505	### Evidence
506	
507	| Artifact | Link / ID |
508	|---|---|
509	| Culprit commit + sessions (Entire) | [dece484 on Entire](https://entire.io/gh/FaridMahmudlu/neathack-agent/commit/dece4846baaed3c5961447af4c0d99a7dd273ed1) |
510	| Checkpoint — benign change | `01M4K1KECVQ0VNT4GVGB9KCB90` (`f4df4da`) |
511	| Checkpoint — bug introduced | `01M4K1P5A9NYJJNRY2D9XKJ08P` (`dece484`) |
512	| Checkpoint — fix | `01M4K1V2G1WYATMGMNK0ZP2KQH` (`63e69d5`) |
513	| neatlogs trace — bugged run | `98330b2d046133fee546ecfc1c011915` |
514	| neatlogs trace — Autopsy's own investigation | `62c2dce9659d83e26711fe123e8c3dc7` |
515	| neatlogs trace — verified fixed run | `ead5a98e094a5e2495f6e428c41fc196` |
516	
517	A nice side-effect captured by the checkpoints: the coding agent (OpenCode +
518	Claude Haiku) was asked twice to introduce the regression as a "refactor"
519	and *refused* — it negated the score instead of flipping the order,
520	preserving correct behaviour. The bug only landed when asked as a debugging
521	experiment. The transcripts tell that whole story; Autopsy reads them.
522	
523	## Layout
524	
525	```
526	agent_debugger/   the debugger agent
527	  neatlogs_api.py   read-only neatlogs Public API client
528	  entire_cli.py     subprocess wrapper for `entire` CLI + graph plugin
529	  tools.py          10 agent tools, each a neatlogs TOOL span
530	  agent.py          investigation loop (WORKFLOW root span)
531	demo_agent/       target system: a tiny research agent we broke on purpose
532	common/           shared LLM client (LiteLLM/Claude) + tool-call loop
533	config.py         dotenv + neatlogs init
534	opencode.json     OpenCode provider config (hackathon LiteLLM proxy)
535	```
536	
537	## How it works
538	
539	Autopsy is an LLM agent loop (Claude Sonnet 4.6) with 14 tools:
540	
541	| Tool | Evidence source |
542	|---|---|
543	| `list_recent_traces`, `inspect_trace`, `read_span_payload`, `compare_traces`, `find_similar_failures` | neatlogs Public API |
544	| `list_checkpoints`, `inspect_checkpoint`, `read_checkpoint_transcript` | Entire checkpoints |
545	| `search_code`, `show_commit_changes` | Entire graph |
546	| `list_recent_commits`, `show_commit_diff`, `read_source_file` | git + source |
547	| `write_diagnosis` | emits `diagnosis.json` |
548	
549	## Monitor mode: `--watch`
550	
551	Run Autopsy as a regression gate — it polls neatlogs and auto-investigates
552	every newly finished trace:
553	
554	```bash
555	.venv/Scripts/python -m agent_debugger --watch 30 --repo .
556	```
557	
558	Add `--fix` to let it repair regressions on its own (each fix becomes an
559	Entire checkpoint).
560	
561	Method: inspect the trace → find the span where the failure surfaced → read
562	its payload → form a hypothesis → locate the implicated code → walk the
563	checkpoints to find which commit/session introduced it → emit the diagnosis
564	with pointers a human can verify.
565	
566	## Closed loop: `--fix` and `--verify`
567	
568	Autopsy doesn't stop at the diagnosis. With `--fix` it hands the suggested
569	fix to an OpenCode coding session — so the *fix itself* lands as its own
570	Entire checkpoint — commits, and with `--verify` re-runs the target agent
571	to confirm. Proven live: commit `4663486` (checkpoint
572	`01M4K6CBKM821B6WC4YCNWE81Z`) is a fix Autopsy diagnosed, had applied, and
573	verified — including a regression test the fix session added on its own.
574	
575	```bash
576	.venv/Scripts/python -m agent_debugger "the flag answer was incomplete" \
577	  --fix --verify ".venv/Scripts/python -m demo_agent \"your question\""
578	```
579	
580	## Setup
581	
582	```bash
583	python -m venv .venv
584	.venv/Scripts/pip install -r requirements.txt        # Git Bash
585	# .venv\Scripts\pip install -r requirements.txt      # cmd/PowerShell
586	cp .env.example .env   # fill in the keys
587	```
588	
589	| Key | Where |
590	|---|---|
591	| `NEATLOGS_API_KEY` | neatlogs → Settings → API keys → **Project API key** |
592	| `NEATLOGS_TOKEN` | neatlogs → Settings → Service Accounts → token with `context:read` + `observability:read` |
593	| `NEATLOGS_PROJECT_ID` | project UUID (dashboard URL / service-account binding) |
594	| `LITELLM_API_KEY` | hackathon LiteLLM proxy key, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (`LITELLM_BASE_URL`) |
595	
596	## Run
597	
598	```bash
599	# the research agent — its runs appear as 'demo-research-agent' traces
600	.venv/Scripts/python -m demo_agent "Which city is the capital of Azerbaijan
601	and what does its flag look like?"
602	
603	# the debugger investigates a run (by trace id or by description)
604	.venv/Scripts/python -m agent_debugger "trace 98330b2d... returned an
605	incomplete answer about the flag" --repo .
606	```
607	
608	## Hackathon sponsor usage
609	
610	- **neatlogs** — both agents are fully traced; the debugger also *reads*
611	  traces back through the Public API as a core tool
612	- **Entire** — every code change is linked to its coding-agent session via
613	  checkpoints; the debugger uses checkpoint explain + transcripts + graph to
614	  attribute bugs to sessions
615	- **cfo.ai** — business plan in [CFO_PLAN.md](CFO_PLAN.md) (pricing, unit
616	  economics, runway)
617

content.content:
a one-repo installation token, applies exactly `fix.patch` on the fetched commit, pushes `resurgo/fix-<run_id>` through an env-var credential helper, opens the PR and writes `pr` into `result.json`. Dry-run checked on the agent-arena and rinne records; the real path has never run, because the App key is not on this machine.

- Agent v2 (`__version__` 0.2.0). Why: the v1 held-out sweep fixed none of the repos that were broken, and the run records show three causes. (1) 6 of 9 broken repos stopped at the model's first "code" proposal, because v1 never applied code fixes (a Foundry test on the removed `testFail*` convention, a turbo.json build-order fix, a package.json dependency change). (2) 2 repos are Bun workspaces with `workspace:*` dependencies and were installed with npm, which rejects the protocol. (3) pnpm repos with `lockfileVersion: '9.0'` and no `packageManager` got the latest pnpm (12), which fails on ERR_PNPM_IGNORED_BUILDS and ignores `pnpm.*` settings; the model then burned attempts migrating settings. What changed:
  - Code fixes are verified, then held. A "code" proposal, or a config proposal that touches a non-config package.json key or a file outside `CONFIG_NAMES`, is applied in the agent container and re-run like a config fix; the attempt is `needs_approval: true` with `approval_reason`, and the record carries `needs_approval`. A lockfile with model-written content or invalid JSON is still rejected as malformed. `pr.refusal()` refuses such records ("this fix changes code and waits for the owner's approval"). The sweep summary splits verified fixes into "PR-ready (config)" and "awaiting approval (code)", plus "no fix needed". The SYSTEM prompt now says this, still prefers config, and forbids passing a step by removing, skipping or weakening a test, build or check.
  - Bun: detected from `bun.lock`, `bun.lockb` or a `packageManager: bun@` field (the field wins over another lockfile). Installed in the toolchain step with `npm install --prefix $HOME/.pm bun@<declared or 1>` (no root); `bun install --frozen-lockfile` / `bun install`; scripts run with `bun run`. The version is only passed to the shell if it is a plain release number.
  - pnpm lockfile 9.0 now maps to pnpm 9.15.9 when there is no `packageManager` field. Caveat: pnpm 10 also writes 9.0, so a repo written by pnpm 10 gets pnpm 9 as well.
  - `trace_id` (the neatlogs trace id of the run's root span, 32 hex characters) is saved in result.json. It comes from the span yielded by `neatlogs.trace()` (`get_span_context().trace_id`); OpenTelemetry's global current span is empty because neatlogs uses its own provider, so that route does not work. Checked with a dummy key (valid id, child spans share it) and on a real run.
  - Pruning: after a pass with more than one applied attempt, files only the non-passing attempts touched are reverted, the pipeline re-runs once, and the smaller patch is kept only if it passes; recorded as `agent.pruned` (`files`, `kept`). The verifier checks the final patch. Not yet exercised: no dev run passed after more than one applied attempt, so this path has never run, in a container or in a unit test.
- v2 development results (sweep `v2-dev`; v1 numbers are from the 2b/2c tables above, so v1 and v2 differ in time caps for sentry-somnia):

| Repo | v1 | v2 | v2 time | v2 model calls | v2 notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Timidan/rinne | runs, 433s, 3 calls | runs | 374s (345s standalone) | 0 | pnpm 9.15.9 rule fixes install on the first attempt |
| Timidan/sentry-somnia | broken (build, 15 min cap), 0 calls | broken (test), 1 call | 1619s (1596s standalone) | 1 (0 standalone) | build now passes; `packages/sentry-react` vitest hits its 5000 ms timeout; the 25-minute budget was spent by two 5-15 minute builds before the model could diagnose in the standalone run |
| Timidan/agent-arena `commentator` | broken (serve), 2 calls, code held | broken (serve), code verified | 861s | 4 | two code fixes (package.json dependency, start script) applied and re-run, held for approval; still failing at serve after the 4-attempt budget |
| buqiyuan/electron-vite-monorepo | runs_with_gaps, 1 call | broken | 299s | 1 | regression: the model proposed a code change whose `apps/electron/package.json` was not valid JSON, so it was rejected as malformed; v1 got a config `.npmrc` fix from the same prompt |
| chroxify/feedbase | runs_with_gaps, 2286s | runs_with_gaps | 1971s | 0 | no test script |
| Timidan/NFTLIL | runs | runs | 191s | 0 | |
| sharkdp/hexyl | runs | runs | 408s | 0 | |

  Sweep totals: 7 repos, 4 verified (3 runs, 1 runs_with_gaps), median 408s, 6 model calls; verified PR-ready (config) 1, awaiting approval (code) 0, no fix needed 3. The v2 changes show up on the repos they target: rinne is fixed by a rule with no model call, and code fixes are now verified rather than abandoned. They did not turn any broken dev repo into a verified one, and electron-vite-monorepo got worse through model variance, not through a changed rule.
- Not done: a Bun workspace repo for the dev set. The session could not search GitHub (network lookups from the shell and web search needed approval that was not available), so no repo was pinned, and the Bun install path has not run on a real repo. The held-out sweep was not run.

## Demo
Not available yet.

## Known limitations and next steps
- Foundry and Rust each have one real run that passed without a fix; the repair loop has not run on either.
- A `start` script that opens no port passes as a "service" after 30 seconds alive, which is a weaker proof than GET /; a web app that takes longer than 30 seconds to open its port would be recorded as a service.
- Monorepos get the library proof bar (install, build, test); their apps are not started.
- The patch is cumulative unless pruning (v2) applies: it only reverts files that failed attempts alone touched, and it has not run in a container yet.
- Bun support has never run on a real repo.
- A rule that fires after a late test failure re-runs install and build, which can spend the whole budget before the model sees the failure (sentry-somnia).
- Reruns always start from install. Lockfile regeneration (an empty-content lockfile entry) and npm pins are implemented but have not been exercised on a real repo.
- The 25-minute Node budget covers the fix loop, not the verifier. Many per-file `docker exec` calls on the remote host made runs slow before reads were batched.
- The `resurgo-runs` network is created if missing and left in place after runs.

## Submission
Confirmed requirements (neatlogs.com/hackathon): public repo with commits dated inside the event; demo video of three minutes or less covering neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai; evidence for the agent improving, failure recovery, neatlogs traces, Entire checkpoints and the cfo.ai plan; building in public tagged #neatHack; submission as a quote post on X, 12 Oct, 19:00–23:55 IST. Entire's submission also needs an accessible checkpoint link and ID.

=================== shivam-taneja__friction-fixer README
# Friction Fixer

An AI agent that fixes your website by itself.

It looks at how visitors behave, changes the page to fix what is driving them away, then checks if the change helped. If it did not help, the agent undoes the change and tries something else.

Built for [neatHack](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon) (Oct 10-12, 2026).

## The problem

Visitors land on a homepage, scroll a bit, and leave. Someone has to read the analytics, guess what is wrong, edit the page, and wait to see if it worked. This is slow and most small teams never do it.

## How it works

Full details are in [FLOW.md](FLOW.md). In short:

1. **Analyst agent** reads the visitor data and writes a plan: what is wrong and one change to try.
2. **Builder agent** reads the plan, edits the site, and opens a pull request (PR).
3. The PR is merged and the site goes live automatically.
4. **Reviewer agent** checks the live site and the new numbers, then decides: keep the change or undo it.
5. If undone, the reason goes back to the Analyst, who tries a different idea.

## Current status

The goal right now is a complete, working loop. Because real traffic takes too long to collect in a 48-hour hackathon, the agent is currently fed **mock visitor data**.

## Project structure

- `agent/` — Python agents that run the loop. Files are placeholders.
- `demo-site/` — the site the Builder is allowed to edit.
- `web/` — the marketing site and the dashboard. How to run it is in [web/README.md](web/README.md).
- `FLOW.md` — what each agent receives and hands on.
- `agent/.env` — agent API keys and the GitHub token. Copy from `agent/.env.example`. Never commit this file.
- `web/.env` — Firebase and cookie secrets for the site. Copy from `web/.env.example`. Never commit this file.
- `.python-version` — tells pyenv to use Python 3.13 in this folder only.

## Setup

Python **3.13** is required. `neatlogs` does not install on 3.14. The `.python-version` file in this repo is set to `3.13`, so this project uses 3.13 and the rest of your machine stays on whatever global version you already have.

You also need git, and a virtualenv named `venv` in the repo root. `venv/` is gitignored.

Fill in `agent/.env` after you copy it. It needs `NEATLOGS_API_KEY`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, `LLM_PROVIDER`, and that provider's API key. The site uses its own file, `web/.env`.

Run the loop from the repo root, with the virtualenv activated:

```bash
python -m agent
```

### Mac

Install [Homebrew](https://brew.sh), then pyenv:

```bash
brew install pyenv
```

Add this to `~/.zshrc`, then open a new terminal:

```bash
export PYENV_ROOT="$HOME/.pyenv"
export PATH="$PYENV_ROOT/bin:$PATH"
eval "$(pyenv init - zsh)"
```

From the repo root:

```bash
pyenv install 3.13
python --version
python -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate
pip install -r agent/requirements.txt
cp agent/.env.example agent/.env
```

`python --version` should print `3.13.x`.

### Windows

Install [pyenv-win](https://github.com/pyenv-win/pyenv-win) in PowerShell:

```powershell
Invoke-WebRequest -UseBasicParsing -Uri "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pyenv-win/pyenv-win/master/pyenv-win/install-pyenv-win.ps1" -OutFile "./install-pyenv-win.ps1"; &"./install-pyenv-win.ps1"
```

Close the terminal and open a new one. pyenv-win needs a full version number, so install one and write that exact version into `.python-version` (for example `3.13.2`):

```powershell
pyenv install -l
pyenv install 3.13.2
cd path\to\friction-fixer
python --version
python -m venv venv
venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r agent/requirements.txt
copy agent\.env.example agent\.env
```

`python --version` should print `3.13.x`.

## Tools used

- **neatlogs:** records every agent run so failures can be found and fixed.
- **Entire:** saves the reasoning behind every code change as checkpoints.
- **cfo.ai:** used to plan pricing, costs and revenue for Friction Fixer as a product.

## Evidence

- neatlogs traces, before vs after improving the agent: _link_
- A run where the agent's change failed and it undid it: _link_
- Website results, before vs after (mock data): _numbers_
- Entire checkpoints: _link or screenshot_
- cfo.ai business plan: _link_
- Demo video: _link_
- Posts shared while building (#neatHack): _links_

# Niyam rulebook

Welfare scheme eligibility rules for Maharashtra, written as tested code.
Every rule links to the clause of the government order it comes from, and
every change is made by the [Niyam agent](https://github.com/usv240/niyam)
with its full reasoning saved as an [Entire](https://entire.io) checkpoint.

| Folder | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `schemes/` | Conditions and benefits of each scheme, each with a source quote |
| `parameters/` | Limits such as ages and income ceilings, with dated values |
| `tests/` | Test citizens with expected results, each citing its clause |
| `sources/` | The official government orders (PDF) |
| `glossary/` | How recurring legal phrases are interpreted |

## Use it

```bash
pip install -e .
python -m niyam_rulebook test                     # run every test citizen
python -m niyam_rulebook rules mh.ladki_bahin --date 2024-06-30
python -m niyam_rulebook simulate '{"age": 34, "gender": "female", "annual_family_income": 240000}' --date 2024-07-01
```

Information only. Final eligibility is always decided by the government department.

# PatchPilot

An agent that fixes bugs in a GitHub-style issue: it reads the issue, runs the tests, asks Gemini for a fix, applies it, and re-runs the tests. If a test still fails or the model call errors (e.g. 503), it retries. Every step is traced with neatlogs. Built for #neathack.

## How it works
1. Read the issue and the buggy file.
2. Run the tests (they fail).
3. Ask Gemini for a fix and write it to the file.
4. Re-run the tests; retry on failure or model error.
5. Print `RESULT: fixed` when tests pass.

## Run it
```bash
python3.12 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install "neatlogs[google-genai]" python-dotenv pytest requests
echo "NEATLOGS_API_KEY=..." >> .env
echo "GEMINI_API_KEY=..." >> .env
python run.py text_utils.py demo_repo/issue2.txt
```

## Demo
`demo_repo/text_utils.py` has 3 bugs (`word_count`, `is_palindrome`, `most_common`).
`./reset_demo.sh` restores the buggy version; then run the command above and watch the tests go from 3 failed to all passed.

## Tracing
`neatlogs.init()` runs before the `google.genai` import, so Gemini calls are traced under the `patchpilot_fix` workflow span.

## Stack
Python, Gemini (google-genai), neatlogs, pytest.

## Sponsor tools
- neatlogs: traces for the agent run (workflow span + Gemini LLM span with input/output, tokens, cost)
- Entire: checkpoints enabled for this repo

=================== DevGajjar28__neatlogs-agents README
# SignalSDR

Outbound agent for neatHack 2026. It researches a seller, finds lookalike buyers, and drafts email that can be sent only when each factual claim has a source. Demo mode never delivers to a real prospect.

## Setup

Python 3.11 or newer.

```bash
py -3.11 -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -e ".[dev]"
copy .env.example .env
```

Fill `.env` locally. `AWS_PROFILE` and `AWS_REGION` select the Bedrock profile. `LLM_MODEL_STRONG` and `LLM_MODEL_FAST` are Bedrock model IDs. No access keys belong in code or in git.

```bash
python cli.py --help
pytest
```

After `.env` is filled, `python cli.py ping-llm` sends one short Bedrock call through neatlogs.

`DATA_MODE=replay` and `DEMO_MODE=true` are the defaults. Replay does not call Crustdata. Demo mode will only hand mail to a local SMTP catcher on `SMTP_HOST` / `SMTP_PORT` (default `localhost:1025`). Docker is not required.

## Commands

```bash
python cli.py run --n 10
python cli.py approve <campaign_id> --yes          # ICP gate, then later email gate
python cli.py serve-ui                             # /icp and /emails
python cli.py worker --once                        # due follow-ups
python cli.py simulate-reply <lead_id>             # stop follow-ups
python cli.py run --narrow-icp                     # force replan.widen_icp
```

`run` stops at ICP, then again at email approval. Demo sends go to Mailpit (`localhost:1025`) as `<lead_id>@sandbox.local`.

## Team

DevGajjar28

## Evidence

- **v0 vs v1:** [`reports/comparison.md`](reports/comparison.md) — PostHog N=10; credits/qualified lead **14.60 → 5.31**; contacts **3 → 10**
- **v1 run:** campaign `v1-posthog-live1` (neatlogs: filter Traces by campaign id; set `NEATLOGS_TRACES_URL` in `.env`)
- **v0 run:** campaign `v0-posthog-live2`
- **Chaos:** `p8-chaos-live2` with `--chaos crust_429,empty_people,llm_bad_json` — events `recovery.llm_bad_json`, `chaos.empty_people`, `recovery.explain_retry`
- **Kill + resume:** `p8-kill1` / `b0-kill-prod` — `kill_after=account_researcher` then `resume` at 0 new credits (cache)
- **Business plan inputs:** [`docs/business-plan/`](docs/business-plan/) (paste into cfo.ai; export PDF/screens there)
- Entire checkpoint: https://entire.io/gh/DevGajjar28/neatlogs-agents/commit/fbc6a690a2013e1288666f3a5e75a8e1c9261aa9 (checkpoint ID: `01M4K32PNHG5B8VRZ6Z7Q2NKVK`)
- Best submission pick: prefer a recovery commit that links a neatlogs failure trace ID in the message (`[trace: <id>]`)

## Limitations

This is a hackathon build. It is not legal advice on outreach. Rules such as GDPR and India's DPDP Act vary by region. Nothing is sent until a verifier and a person approve it, and demo sends stay on the local catcher.

=================== siddarth-ba-72__DataTraceMind README
# DataTraceMind

An agentic data-reliability engineer. It detects when a data pipeline is
producing wrong numbers, investigates the cause with evidence from the source
database, the pipeline, the analytics target, and the approved business
rules, proposes a minimal repair, proves that repair in staging, and applies
it only after a human approves that exact change.

The failure it is built around is the silent one: the ETL job reports
`SUCCESS` while the revenue it loaded is wrong.

Built for neatHack (10–12 October 2026). The build log and submission
evidence are in [hackathon.md](hackathon.md).

## What happens in one incident

1. A simulator writes orders, payments, and refunds to PostgreSQL (`oltp`).
2. A Python ETL loads the analytics schema, driven by a versioned
   transformation file.
3. The Scenario Lab, a separate page for whoever operates the demo, injects
   one known fault.
4. Deterministic quality checks fail and the monitor opens an incident. No
   model decides that something is wrong.
5. A supervisor runs the agent roles: a source-data investigator and a
   pipeline investigator in parallel, a contract lookup, a root-cause analyst,
   and a repair agent. Each model-backed role is one Codex turn with its own
   tool allow-list and output schema.
6. The repair is run in a staging schema against regression fixtures and every
   quality check, and the load is replayed to prove a retry changes nothing.
7. A person reviews the evidence, diff, and staging result, then approves or
   rejects. Approval is bound to the patch hash.
8. On approval the patch is applied, the pipeline reruns, and the incident
   resolves only if every check passes. Otherwise it rolls back.

36	## Run it
37	
38	Requirements: Docker, Python 3.13, Node.js 22 or newer, and the
39	[Codex CLI](https://developers.openai.com/codex/cli) signed in (`codex login`)
40	or `CODEX_API_KEY` set. Without model credentials everything except
41	"Investigate" still works; that button is refused with a message saying why.
42	
43	```sh
44	cp .env.example .env                  # add NEATLOGS_API_KEY to trace agent runs
45	docker compose up -d postgres
46	python3.13 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt
47	(cd frontend && npm install && npm run build)
48	.venv/bin/uvicorn datatracemind.api.app:app --port 8000
49	```

51	The first start seeds a deterministic baseline. There are two pages:
52	
53	| Page | URL | What it is for |
54	|---|---|---|
55	| Incident console | <http://127.0.0.1:8000/> | The product: data trust, incidents, evidence, repair review and approval, audit log |
56	| Scenario Lab | <http://127.0.0.1:8000/lab/> | Operating the demo environment: live traffic, fault injection, reset |
57	
58	The console never injects anything and is never told what was injected; the
59	lab never investigates. Each links to the other.
60	
61	Demo path: in the **Scenario Lab**, pick a scenario, read its briefing, and
62	press **Inject fault**. Follow **Open INC-0001** to the console, then
63	**Investigate → review the repair → Approve and apply**. Back in the lab,
64	**Reset to baseline** returns to the clean state. An investigation takes about
65	a minute and four Codex turns.
66	
67	Live traffic is optional. **Start traffic** in the lab keeps simulated
68	customers writing orders, payments, and refunds to the source at a chosen rate
69	(light, steady, or busy); **Send 25 now** writes one batch instead. Every
70	scenario also reproduces on the seeded baseline with traffic paused, and a
71	reset pauses it so each run starts from the same data.
72	
73	For frontend development, `npm run dev` in `frontend/` serves both pages on
74	port 5173 (`/` and `/lab/`) and proxies `/api` to port 8000.
